title: Bringing Inference Programs To Solana
notes: We’ve written three draft Solana Improvement Documents, SIMDs, to bring inference programs to Solana. Informally, they’re the standard behind what we call Actually Smart Contracts. Here’s the idea, why it matters, and what’s in the drafts.

title: Trustless systems still run on human judgment.
notes: Blockchains have made real progress toward trustless, decentralized systems that run without anyone in charge. But they still lean on people for judgment: discussion, opinion, motives and alignment, all happening off chain. That’s been a steady source of inefficiency, and of risk. A DAO can pass a constitution, but it has no full-time lawyers to enforce it. An insurer can write a policy that a smart contract is meant to pay out on, but deciding whether a claim qualifies still happens off chain, by people. An exchange may want to wrap its hot wallets in procedures that protect user funds, and find it can only enforce what code can express. Code is law, and code can’t say everything. So we think it’s time to talk about how AI and blockchains can converge to add the missing piece: judgment, and policy checks built into the contract itself. A program should be able to get a second opinion, ask an expert panel, or go to a judiciary before it moves funds. That’s why we’re introducing Actually Smart Contracts as three SIMDs for Solana itself.

title: A prompt on chain. Models off chain. A signed, provable answer.
notes: Here’s the whole idea in one paragraph. Store a prompt on chain the way you’d store a program, along with the context that should shape the decision: policies, rules, a constitution, even a link to a DAO discussion. Let any Solana program call it. AI models run it off chain, and each one signs the result on chain: we ran this program, at this version, on this input, and this is the answer. A proof of inference shows which model actually did the thinking. The calling program checks the signatures before it acts. That changes what a smart contract can be. Today a program can only enforce what code can express. With an inference program, it can enforce a sentence like “the treasury shall not fund political campaigns.”

title: Each side does what it’s best at.
notes: Proof of inference is the key because it lets each side do what it’s best at. Solana does what blockchains do best. It keeps a permanent, public record of decisions, certifications and proof statements, and of every payment. It stores the programs and the context the models should use, and lets other programs trigger them. The models do the deep thinking off chain: reading a constitution, weighing evidence, deciding whether an action breaks a rule. That takes large models on serious hardware, and it doesn’t belong on chain. The proof joins them. It shows which model gave the answer, so the chain can trust a decision it didn’t compute. Without it, you’re trusting whoever ran the model. With it, you’re checking. Together, that opens up DAO arbitration, ethics checks for models and agents, policy checks, certifications and more.

title: Proofs are too big for the chain. Make lying expensive instead.
notes: Here's the hard part. A proof that a specific model produced an answer is the strongest evidence we have, and it doesn't fit on Solana. One proof today is about eighteen point eight megabytes. A transaction holds twelve hundred bytes. Storing one would cost about a hundred and thirty SOL in rent, uploading it would take about nineteen thousand transactions, and verifying it takes seventeen seconds on twenty-four CPU threads, where a transaction gets milliseconds. It covers one open model. And a proof hash the chain can't check proves nothing on its own: anyone could post the hash of a proof that doesn't exist. So instead of the proof, we store three things. A commitment, by hash, to the output, the model, the runtime and the proof, so the evaluator can't change its story. A guarantee that all of it stays fetchable through the challenge window. And a bond, so lying costs money: anyone can challenge a vote by re-running an open model, demanding the proof, or checking a hardware report, and a proven fault loses the bond. That gives a ladder: signatures, then different model families, then bonded and challengeable, then proven by verifiers, and one day, verified on chain, once proofs can be wrapped into something a few hundred bytes long. None of this is new. Oracles, optimistic rollups, optimistic machine learning, proof wrapping, which Solana already verifies with Groth16, and confidential GPUs all work this way today.

title: Two missing pieces.
notes: Why now? Two pieces have been missing. The first is a way to know which model ran. A signature proves which key signed, not which model did the work. Anthropic’s research on provable inference shows a provider can prove that a committed set of model weights produced a specific answer, without revealing the weights. It’s a research prototype today. Proofs run to tens of megabytes and take seconds to verify, for one open model, which is too big for a Solana transaction. So the drafts check proofs off chain and leave room to bring that on chain later. The second missing piece is a common format. Without one, every team invents its own requests, signatures and results, and nothing can read them across applications. That’s what a SIMD is for.

title: Rules that code alone can’t enforce.
notes: What would it make possible? Constitutions that hold: a DAO checks a passed proposal against its constitution before it executes. Treasury guardrails: a withdrawal over a threshold waits for a ruling against a written policy. On-chain certifications: a published standard becomes a program, models review a specific commit against it, and the ruling is a public certificate. Prediction markets: independent models record a signed forecast before the event, and a separate ruling resolves the market after it. And agent policies: programs acting for AI agents check risky actions against the agent’s written limits. For an example of what we have in mind, look at Verafy Judiciary at judiciary.verafy.ai. You write your community’s rules once, and a jury of AI models from different companies applies them to a dispute and cites the clause behind each ruling. These SIMDs are how rulings like that could be recorded on chain, proven, and acted on by any Solana program.

title: Six pieces, three SIMDs.
notes: So what’s actually in the drafts? Six pieces, across three SIMDs. The first SIMD, Inference Programs, covers the first three. The second, Evaluators and Attestations, covers four and five. The third, Rulings, Disputes and Challenges, covers six. One, instructions: what the inference program is for and the outcomes it’s allowed to return, stored on chain in whatever form is smallest or most private. Two, internal context: the program’s own rules, like a DAO constitution or bill of rights, run rules, an insurance policy or certification standards, stored inline, pulled from a web page, or pulled from a trusted GitHub repository pinned at a commit. Three, calls: each call injects a request prompt, the question; external context, the evidence; jury shaping, which models, how many and what level of proof; and an escrowed payment that pays the model providers, with refunds and a top-up callback. Four, evaluators: model operators register a signing key, their prices, and a commitment to exactly what they run. Five, attestations: signed votes bound to one request and its exact inputs, committed before they’re revealed. Six, rulings: the contract writes back a signed decision, like a court opinion, with a summary, reasoning, sources, certainty, every model’s wallet signature, and a co-signed sign-off.

title: Anatomy of an Actually Smart Contract
notes: Here’s what an Actually Smart Contract contains, and what flows into it. In the middle is the inference program, on chain. It holds its instructions, what it’s for, the outcomes it’s allowed to return, its jury minimums and proof floor, how changeable it is, its context budget, and a safe default. On the right are its own materials, its internal context: a DAO constitution or bill of rights, run rules, an insurance policy. Those can be stored inline, pulled from a web page, or pulled from a trusted GitHub repository pinned at a specific commit. On the left is everything a caller injects for one request: a request prompt, the question for this call; external context, the evidence, as links, text or documents; jury shaping, which models, what quorum and what level of proof; and payment, an escrowed budget that pays the model providers and refunds what’s left. The evaluators run off chain, read the instructions, the internal context and the external context, vote with proofs, and get paid from escrow. The result is a signed ruling: the decision, reasoning, sources, certainty and wallet signatures, returned to the caller. Internal context is the rules. External context is the case. The case never overrides the rules.

title: Calling an Actually Smart Contract
notes: Here’s what a smart contract sends when it calls an Actually Smart Contract. First, it can inject context for that one call: a link, which gets snapshotted, a paragraph of text, or documents to check, like the proposal being judged or the claim being made. External context never overrides the internal rules. Second, it shapes the jury: which labs and which models are allowed, how many evaluators and what quorum, and what level of proof is required, from signatures only up to verified proofs of inference. A request can narrow the program’s jury, never widen it. Third, it pays for it. It asks for a quote first, an estimate of what the inference will cost. Then it escrows a budget. When the evaluators reveal their votes, each one is paid at the price it published, to its own wallet, and whatever is left is refunded. If the budget runs short, say a proof costs more than expected, the request pauses, the caller gets a callback saying it needs funds, and anyone can top it up. If no one does, it expires to the safe default and the rest is refunded.

title: What goes into a request
notes: Here's everything that goes into a request, the RulingRequest account a caller creates when it asks an inference program for a ruling. The caller is a Solana program calling in by cross-program invocation, or a user. First, the pinned rules: when the request is created it copies the program's revision, its prompt hash and its context hash, so later edits to the program never apply to this request. Second, the question: the request prompt, up to a kilobyte, plus a hash of the exact action being judged and the evidence. Third, external context: up to eight documents, links that get snapshotted, text or files, plus a short note. They are the case, and they never override the program's own rules. Fourth, jury shaping: how many evaluators, the quorum, the assurance level from signatures up to proofs, and which model families and models are allowed. A request can narrow the jury, never widen it. Fifth, payment: the quote, the budget escrowed in this account, fee caps, what's been spent and where the refund goes. Sixth, callbacks and the clock: which program gets told when the ruling is final, needs funds, expired or disputed, and the deadlines for deadlines and top-up. The whole account is under three kilobytes, and its rent comes back when the request is closed.

title: What the contract writes back: a signed ruling
notes: So what does an Actually Smart Contract write back to the chain? Not just yes or no. It writes a signed ruling, like a court opinion. At the top: the decision, here allow, with the assurance level it reached. The certainty: how strongly the models agreed, here five of five, with their own confidence scores. And the pinned hashes of the exact prompt, internal context, external context and input it ruled on. In the middle: a short summary of the decision, the full reasoning stored by hash and reference, and the sources it used. Every source has to hash to one of the pinned context documents or evidence items, so a ruling can’t cite a document the models were never given. At the bottom: a wallet signature from every model that voted, the sign-off, where one model writes the opinion and the others co-sign it, and any dissents, which stay on the record. Then the program calls ReadRuling and gets back the outcome, assurance, agreement, confidence and summary hash, checks it, and acts. These values are illustrative.

title: What a ruling records on chain
notes: This is exactly what a ruling records on chain, field by field, with the bytes each part takes. A header that links it to its request and its inference program. The four pinned hashes: the prompt, the internal context, the external context and the input, so anyone can see exactly what was ruled on. The decision: the outcome, the assurance level actually reached, the status and the slot. Certainty: how many agreed, how many answered, and their confidence. The opinion: which evaluator wrote it, a summary of up to 512 bytes inline, and a hash and reference for the full reasoning. Up to sixteen sources, each checked on chain against what the jury was given, so a ruling can't cite a document that wasn't in the record. Then the signatures: one wallet signature per counted vote, a sign-off from each agreeing evaluator over the opinion, and any dissents. The long material stays off chain by hash: the full reasoning, every evaluator's output, proofs of inference and dissent statements. A calling program gets a compact answer back from ReadRuling: the outcome, the assurance, the agreement, the confidence and the summary hash. At the fixed layout it's about six kilobytes; sized to what a typical ruling uses, it's under two.

title: Any ruling can be challenged. None is erased.
notes: Rulings aren't final forever, and they shouldn't be. Here's how a ruling gets challenged. Ruling R1 denies a claim, relying on two sources. A few days later it's disputed, re-judged on the same evidence by different model families, and upheld. Years later, new evidence emerges: one of those sources is corrected, or a forgery comes to light. Anyone the program allows can open a challenge, at any time, with no deadline. The challenge is a new ruling, R2. Its jury gets the original ruling and its full reasoning, the original evidence, and the new material, clearly labeled as new, and it has to compare itself to R1, source by source. Here it overturns it. Just as a Supreme Court decision can be overturned eighty years later, but stays in the books, R1 is never erased. It stays on chain, marked overturned, with a link to the ruling that overturned it. A challenge needs grounds: new evidence, false evidence, rules that were misapplied, or rules that have since changed. The result is affirmed, overturned, superseded under new rules, or, with no quorum, R1 simply stands. And there are guards against relitigating until you win: the challenger posts a bond, returned only if they win; every challenge has to bring something new; each review uses fresh model families; and the jury gets larger. Past actions stay settled on chain. What changes is the record, and what programs do next: an insurer can pay a claim whose denial was overturned, and no program can act on an overturned ruling.

title: A forecast on record before the event. A ruling after it.
notes: Inference programs can make predictions as well as judgments, and that makes them a natural fit for prediction markets. Before the market closes, the market, or anyone, requests a forecast ruling: the market's question is the request prompt, say, will the Fed cut rates on December tenth, and the external context is the evidence: news, filings, a forum thread, all snapshotted. Each model votes yes or no with a probability. The votes are signed, committed before they're revealed, and timestamped on chain, so there's a public record of what independent models expected, before the event. After the event, a separate resolver program rules on what actually happened. Its internal context holds the market's resolution rules, what counts and which sources decide, and its external context is the official statement. The market pays out after the dispute window. Any time later, a program can read both rulings and score how well each model forecast, and a resolution can be challenged and overturned on new or false sources. We've done the resolution half in a recorded run: a forecast market resolved on the real FOMC statement, six of six. The resolver never sees the forecast, so it can't anchor on it. And a forecast is the models' estimate, never more.

title: System 1 screens. System 2 rules.
notes: Can this be made faster and cheaper? Yes, and the most promising route is a new kind of model. TypeSafe's Jev is what they call a System One model: instead of writing text, it returns a typed answer, a choice, a score or a yes or no, with a calibrated probability, in 70 to 500 milliseconds and for about four hundredths of a cent, by the vendor's numbers. Think of it like the two systems in the human mind. System 1 is the fast gut check. System 2 is slow, careful reasoning. In an inference program, System 1 screens and System 2 rules. Every request first goes through a fast screen, one yes or no question per rule. If the answer is clear and the stakes are low, the caller gets a fast result, or the safe default. If it's unclear or the stakes are high, it escalates to the full jury, which takes 20 to 60 seconds and about half a cent. The pluses: it's sub-second, so it fits inside an agent's loop or a withdrawal flow. Its typed answers map straight onto the outcomes a program lists. Its probabilities are calibrated, which is better than a language model telling you how confident it feels. And each rule in a constitution becomes a yes or no question checked in parallel. The minuses: it gives no reasoning, so it can't write the opinion or cite the sources a ruling needs. It's one hosted, closed model, so there's no diversity of labs and no proof of inference. On the vendor's own benchmark it scores 67.8 percent against 73 to 74 for frontier models. And calibrated doesn't mean correct; it's weaker on numbers and on questions that bundle several judgments. So System 1 is the fast lane, not the court.

title: Models don’t need tidy English.
notes: A few design choices make this practical. First, it’s small. Models don’t need tidy English. A prompt can be written in any language and compiled into a terse form a model still reads directly. One of our 178-byte withdrawal rules compiles to 68 bytes. On top of that, content can be compressed. Our five draft standards, about 3,400 words, compress to about 5 kilobytes, roughly four hundredths of a SOL in rent. Second, it’s private if you want. Content can be encrypted so only the chosen evaluators can read it, and everyone else sees a hash. The evaluators decompress and decrypt before the model sees anything. Third, it’s changeable. The creator can update both the prompt and its context at any time, stage changes behind a public delay, or freeze them for good. Every ruling pins the exact hashes it used, so a change never rewrites a past decision. The real limit isn’t storage, it’s the model’s context window, so each program declares a context budget.

title: Honest limits.
notes: And what it doesn’t do. It doesn’t change the validator: everything in the drafts can be built as a Solana program today. It doesn’t verify proofs of inference on chain, because they’re still too big, so registered verifiers check them off chain. And it doesn’t make models infallible. In our tests, a forged correction in the evidence fooled all ten models we tried. The drafts say so, and ask calling programs to keep hard limits in their own code.

title: Open the idea to Solana. Find out if it’s viable.
notes: So what’s next? Solana’s SIMD process asks that ideas be discussed before a proposal is submitted. We’re opening a discussion in the SIMD repository’s Ideas section to find out whether this is viable, what’s wrong with it, and who wants to build it with us. All three drafts are on the Verafy blog, and you can see Actually Smart Contracts run at asc.verafy.ai. Tell us where it’s wrong.
